source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (Study 1)
finding: A crowd of 12 different LLMs, median per question, matched a human forecasting crowd. This is a cross-model crowd, not a single-model crowd within.
numbers: 31 binary Metaculus questions; each of 12 models queried 3 times at default settings. LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.85; LLM crowd beat the 0.25 no-information benchmark, t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026.
limits: Only 31 questions; web interfaces, default temperature; models differ in size and search access. Not a same-model test.
agent_relevance: Aggregation over different models helps. Aggregation over samples of one model is a weaker case because errors are shared (see c18).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (model table, acquiescence)
finding: Individual models were uneven and biased upward. The median across models cancelled much of the bias.
numbers: Per-model Brier in one subset table ran from 0.075 (GPT-4) to 0.212 (Coral); aggregate 0.041 on that subset. Mean model forecasts were significantly above 50% although resolutions were nearly an even split.
limits: Subset tables are small and not comparable to the 0.20 headline.
agent_relevance: Use the median, not the mean, when samples may share a lean. Expect a common bias to survive averaging.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (Study 2, update toward human median)
finding: Showing a model the human median improved it, but a plain average of model and human beat the model's own update.
numbers: 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts. GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001). Simple average of machine and human: GPT-4 0.13, Claude 2 0.14; updates significantly worse than that average (t(92)=2.58, p=.011; t(92)=3.53, p=.001). Update size correlated with initial gap, r=0.88 and 0.87.
limits: Human median came from a tournament with many informed people. The mix is human plus machine, not self plus self.
agent_relevance: Models move toward a shown number but under-use it. Averaging in code beats asking the model to blend. Matches guardrail G5.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (interval width)
finding: Models narrowed their stated range after seeing the human median, as theory predicts.
limits: Intervals were self-stated and not scored for calibration here.
agent_relevance: Stated ranges are cheap to collect and respond to evidence; they may serve as a spread signal.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (headline gains)
finding: Sample many reasoning paths from one model and take the majority answer. This is the main machine form of the crowd within, and it gives large gains on tasks with a checkable final answer.
numbers: 40 sampled paths. Absolute gains over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
limits: Answers must be comparable by exact match. Gains shrink as the greedy baseline gets stronger.
agent_relevance: The closest existing method to the crowd within for our agent. Gains are real when the answer space is small and checkable.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (model-size table)
finding: Gain varies by model and task: big on weak or mid baselines, small near ceiling.
limits: 2022 models; modern models may already be near ceiling on these sets.
agent_relevance: Expect small gains from resampling on items the model already gets right most of the time.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (vs other ensembles)
finding: Resampling one model beat mixing prompts and mixing models. Weak models in a mixed ensemble dragged it down.
numbers: GSM8K, PaLM-540B: SC x40 74.4; 40 prompt sets 58.9; 40 prompt permutations 59.6; SC plus different prompt sets 75.4. Mixed-model ensembles scored 16.0 to 36.9.
limits: Mixed ensembles here were crude (very different model strengths).
agent_relevance: Within-model sampling is a strong baseline. Extra prompt variety added about +1 over SC alone here.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (consistency as confidence)
finding: The share of samples that agree with the final answer tracks accuracy. SC also beat sample-and-rank at the same sample count.
numbers: Agreement rate correlated strongly with GSM8K accuracy (Figure 5). Sample-and-rank gained less than SC for the same number of samples on GPT-3 code-davinci-001 (Figure 3).
quote: consistency ... is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: Agreement is a hint; shared errors still produce confident wrong majorities.
agent_relevance: Agreement rate is a free signal for an impasse detector, but never proof (G4).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (ensembling sweep)
finding: Averaging 6 sampled forecasts from the same system gave almost nothing. Mean, median and trimmed mean were within 0.003 Brier of no ensembling.
numbers: Validation set, 6 base reasonings. Baseline (no ensemble) 0.1676; mean 0.1656; median 0.1651; geometric mean 0.1655; trimmed mean 0.1649; USC (LLM aggregator) 0.1691, worse than baseline; human crowd 0.1600.
limits: Best gain is 0.0027 Brier, likely inside noise at this validation size. Samples come from a retrieval system with shared news.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for small, correlated gains. An LLM aggregator did worse than plain code averaging (G5).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models (end-to-end test)
finding: The full system (retrieval, tuned prompts, ensemble) approached but did not beat the human crowd. Raw single models were near the no-skill level.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 (system) vs 0.149 (crowd); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best single baseline model GPT-4-1106-Preview 0.208; random 0.250.
limits: Ensembling is one of several parts; most gain came from retrieval and prompting.
agent_relevance: Resampling is a small part of forecast quality; information and prompt design matter more.

source: Jaworski and Alam (2026) Synthetic Consensus: Evaluating LLM Forecasts with Repeated Draws
finding: Averaging 500 repeated draws from one model on inflation forecasts cut error by 7 to 35 percent, and most of the gain came within 10 draws. Stronger models varied less between calls and gained less.
numbers: 500 queries per quarterly inflation forecast, 3 economies, target quarters after the knowledge cutoff. Removable between-call variation is typically 16% of single-response error, up to 76%.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref metadata); preprint; numeric forecasting, not reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Best direct LLM test of the crowd within for numbers. Same pattern as in people: the first few draws give most of the gain, and the gain is bounded by the share of pure noise.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study (low variance)
finding: Strong models repeated the same number across samples, so there is little noise to average away.
numbers: 30 runs per question at temperature 0.8. In 78 of 108 GPT-4 and GPT-4o experiments the standard deviation was almost zero (same number 30 times); for GPT-3.5 only about one quarter had zero spread.
limits: Small question set; one temperature; numeric hint tasks.
agent_relevance: Crowd-within gain needs variance. A confident model gives a crowd of one. Check spread before paying for samples.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study (anchor strength)
finding: Models were anchored by expert hints; debiasing prompts did not fix it. Showing several hints from different angles did help.
numbers: Mean anchoring index for GPT-4 about 0.45, vs 0.61 in the human study the data came from. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, ignore-anchor and reflection prompts did not reduce expert-anchor bias in GPT-4 and GPT-4o.
limits: Authors are high-school students; GPT-4 and 4o only; stock-price style items.
agent_relevance: Anchoring limits any same-context second look. Offering independent hints from different sources works better than telling the model to ignore the first.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Self-debiasing (the model rereads all information at once and may change decisions) worked only for large models. Small models flipped many decisions.
numbers: 13,465-prompt dataset. In the anchoring case Llama models changed 40 to 52% of their decisions when allowed to revise (Table 4). Self-help cut group-attribution bias to 0 for GPT-4 but failed for Llama.
limits: Admissions-decision task, not numeric estimates.
agent_relevance: A second look by the model itself is only safe with a strong model. Weak models churn.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind (same-model repetition)
finding: Even at high temperature, one model's samples to open-ended questions are very alike.
numbers: INFINITY-CHAT, 50 responses per query, top-p 0.9, T=1.0, embedding similarity: in 79% of cases mean pairwise similarity exceeds 0.8. With min-p (T=2.0), 81% of pairs exceed 0.7 and 61.2% exceed 0.8.
limits: Embedding similarity of text, not answer correctness.
agent_relevance: Same-model samples are a thin crowd. Do not count them as independent views (G4).

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind (across models)
finding: Different models also converge, so mixing models buys less diversity than hoped.
numbers: Mean pairwise similarity between different models 71% to 82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. 70+ models, 26K queries.
limits: Open-ended chat prompts, not forecasts or math.
agent_relevance: The cross-model fix is also limited; real diversity needs different information or different methods.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized Sampling
finding: Asking the model to list several answers with probabilities in one call restores diversity lost to alignment, without training.
numbers: Creative writing: diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting; human rating +25.7%; recovers 66.8% of the base model's diversity.
limits: Creative tasks; diversity is not accuracy. Gains larger for stronger models.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to get a spread of answers in one call, like a dialectical-bootstrapping prompt. Test on checkable tasks before trusting.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Model errors overlap heavily, and bigger, more accurate models overlap more.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions, 71 on 14,042 (HELM), 20 on 1,800 resume pairs. On one leaderboard models agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong.
limits: Different models, not same-model resamples; multiple choice.
agent_relevance: If different models share errors, resamples of one model share more. Majority vote cannot fix shared errors.

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need
finding: Plain sampling and voting scales with ensemble size across tasks and models.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +12 to +24, MATH +6 to +10, Chess +1 to +4, MMLU +5 to +11, HumanEval +4 to +9 points. Llama2-13B reached 0.59 on GSM8K at size 40, above single Llama2-70B at 0.54; GPT-3.5 GSM8K 0.73 to 0.85.
limits: Gains smaller on hard tasks (MATH, Llama2-13B 0.03 to 0.09); same-model samples.
agent_relevance: Cheap breadth works for answers that can be voted on; it cannot reach what the model never solves.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents (Self-MoA)
finding: Aggregating many samples from one top model beat mixing different models, because mixing lowers average quality.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6% over mixed MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0; +3.8% on average across MMLU, CRUX and MATH. Mixing helps only in some settings.
limits: Aggregation is by an LLM aggregator, which can add its own bias.
agent_relevance: Quality beats diversity at this scale. Start with one strong model resampled.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Sampling finds correct answers far more often than voting or reward models can pick them. Selection is the bottleneck.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples, 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward model: 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (with a verifier). Gemma-2B CodeContests 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000.
limits: Voting plateaus near 100 samples; verifiers are needed for code.
agent_relevance: Majority vote over resamples stalls. Gains beyond a point need a real check (G3), not more votes.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (intrinsic self-correction)
finding: Asking a model to review its own answer with no outside feedback did not help and often hurt. This is the machine form of a second look by the same mind.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after self-correction (3 calls); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 (3 calls) and 89.0 (5 calls). With oracle labels telling it when to revise, GPT-4 GSM8K rose to 97.5 and GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA to 89.7.
limits: Oracle-label gains are not real-world gains.
agent_relevance: A second look in the same context is not a second sample. Only fresh sampling or real feedback helps (G2).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (debate vs self-consistency)
finding: Multi-agent debate did not beat majority vote at an equal number of responses.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: single response 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate rounds scored 83.2 and 83.0 in the table, and the paper states debate significantly underperforms SC at equal responses.
limits: Table layout was garbled in text extraction; only the SC rows and the prose claim are used with confidence.
agent_relevance: Debate costs more and adds no edge over plain voting.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several copies of one model that read each other's answers and revise beat a single agent and plain majority.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8; grade-school math: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0; chess pawn score 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Later work (c23) shows equal-budget voting closes most of the gap.
agent_relevance: Interaction among copies may add a little beyond voting but also risks shared drift.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) The Effect of Sampling Temperature on Problem Solving in LLMs
finding: Raising temperature from 0.0 to 1.0 did not change single-answer accuracy significantly, so temperature is a safe lever for sample spread.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 5 prompt techniques; Kruskal-Wallis for GPT-3.5 CoT on a 1,000-question exam H(10)=10.439, p=0.403. Performance fell rapidly above 1.0 and was incoherent at 1.6.
limits: Multiple-choice exams; single-sample accuracy, not ensembles.
agent_relevance: Use temperature up to about 1.0 to widen samples at no per-sample cost; do not rely on it for real diversity (c15).

source: Arora et al. (2022) Ask Me Anything: A simple strategy for prompting language models
finding: Many noisy prompt formats of one model, combined with weak supervision that models their dependencies, beat plain majority.
numbers: Average lift 10.2% over few-shot baseline for GPT-J-6B; on RTE-style tasks majority vote lift 3.7 points vs weak supervision 6.1 points; 41% average improvement over few-shot on 20 tasks for GPT-3 175B comparisons.
limits: Prompt-format variety rather than sampling noise; needs a label model.
agent_relevance: Votes from one model are dependent; weighting for dependence beat counting. Same lesson as G4.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: A dialectical-bootstrapping style patch (ask logically related questions and reconcile the forecasts) raised consistency but not accuracy.
numbers: ArbitrageForecaster improved consistency on the checks it optimised, did not generalise to held-out checks, and did not improve forecasting performance. 10 consistency rules (negation, paraphrase and others).
limits: Result as stated by the authors in the introduction.
agent_relevance: Making answers agree with each other is not the same as making them right. Consistency is a check, not a fix.

source: Naik et al. (2023) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Varying the approach in the prompt, not just the token noise, gave more than same-prompt sampling. This is the machine form of dialectical bootstrapping.
numbers: GPT-4 AQuA-RAT +9.84 (few-shot, base 71.9%) and +14.6 (zero-shot, base 70.47%) points; GPT-3.5 +14.23 and +16.52. Blocksworld 3, GPT-4: zero-shot CoT 70%, SC-10 73%, DIV-SE 94%. Blocksworld 4/5: ZS-CoT 40%, SC-10 41.2%. No gain for GPT-3.5 on Blocksworld.
limits: Needs a model able to follow varied approaches; no gain for weak models.
agent_relevance: Different methods per sample can beat identical-prompt resampling on planning. G4 warns against persona voters on single-answer tasks; test per task.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
finding: A layered mixture of agents reached 65.1% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 versus 57.5% for GPT-4 Omni.
numbers: 65.1% vs 57.5% (the paper text also cites 65.8% in its introduction).
limits: Win rate is judged by an LLM; Self-MoA later showed single-model aggregation can beat it (c20).
agent_relevance: Aggregation by a model reading many drafts works for open text; for answers we still prefer code (G5).
